analysis.one_liner: Guarantees Medicare beneficiaries who lose their coverage can buy a supplemental policy without health-based denials or surcharges.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced in February 1997 and received no further action before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen protections for people with Medicare supplemental (Medigap) insurance. Anyone who loses coverage through no fault of their own — because their Medicare HMO leaves the area or shuts down, their insurer goes bankrupt, they move out of state, or their retiree plan ends — would have the right to buy another Medigap policy within 63 days, with no denial, no surcharge for poor health, and no exclusion of pre-existing conditions. It would also ban preexisting-condition exclusions during the standard six-month signup window when people first turn 65 and enrolled in Medicare, and extend that same six-month open enrollment to disabled beneficiaries under 65. Finally, it would fund up to $35 million a year in grants so consumer groups and state agencies could give beneficiaries plain-language comparisons of Medigap policies and Medicare HMOs, with insurers required to run and disclose customer satisfaction surveys.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries in unstable coverage situations: people whose Medicare HMO exits their area or drops them, whose Medigap insurer becomes insolvent or stops selling, who move to a state where their policy isn't licensed, or whose employer retiree supplement terminates. Also disabled beneficiaries under 65, who would get the same six-month window to buy a policy without preexisting-condition exclusions as people turning 65. Beneficiaries would also get subsidized, standardized information about their plan options.

how_it_helps.text: People who lose coverage involuntarily — HMO exit or contract termination, insurer bankruptcy, insurer closing the block of business to new enrollment, moving out of state, or employer plan termination — would be guaranteed the right to enroll in a comparable or lesser Medigap policy within 63 days, with no denial, no health-based pricing, and no preexisting-condition exclusion [S3].

During the initial six-month enrollment period after first becoming eligible, insurers could not exclude benefits based on a preexisting condition or price the policy based on health status, claims experience, genetic information, or disability [S3].
Disabled beneficiaries under 65 would get the same six-month initial enrollment protection as seniors, with a transition rule and notice for people already eligible before the effective date [S3].

Insurers and Medicare HMOs would have to run consumer satisfaction surveys and turn the results over to the government, and the Secretary would fund grants to nonprofit consumer organizations and state agencies to give beneficiaries complete, uniform comparisons of their plan options, paid for by the industry up to $35 million a year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medigap insurers and Medicare managed care plans. They would have to accept and cover applicants regardless of health status in the protected situations, absorb the risk of sicker enrollees, run satisfaction surveys, notify enrollees of their rights when coverage ends, and pay their pro rata share of the counseling program's cost, capped at $35 million per year. Some of that cost would likely be passed into premiums paid by all Medigap policyholders.

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed issue without health-based pricing means sicker applicants can no longer be turned away or charged more, which tends to raise premiums across the board so healthier policyholders effectively subsidize the protection — a cost that lands partly on the very seniors the bill aims to help [S3].

The portability right is limited: it applies only to a policy with benefits comparable or lesser than the coverage lost, only within a 63-day window, and only for the specific losing-coverage events the bill lists — people who voluntarily drop a policy after the first year, for example, get no guarantee [S3].
The industry-funded counseling program would draw money from insurers' pro rata assessments, a cost that can be passed into premiums, though it is capped at $35 million per fiscal year [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target a real gap: people whose coverage collapses through no fault of their own can otherwise find themselves uninsurable on the individual Medigap market at any price. The limits (comparable-or-lesser benefits, 63-day window, listed events only) keep the mandate narrower than a full guaranteed-issue requirement, and the counseling program is industry-funded rather than adding to the deficit. The main cost is premium pressure on all Medigap policyholders from covering sicker enrollees — a genuine trade-off, but one that falls on the population the bill protects, who gain the right to coverage they can actually keep.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day it was introduced and stayed there — no hearing, no vote, no floor action — until the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. John Chafee introduced the Medigap Portability Act of 1997 on February 11, 1997, joined by four original cosponsors from both parties, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
The action history shows no further activity after the February 11, 1997 committee referral for the remainder of the 105th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medigap insurers and Medicare HMOs, who avoided the guaranteed-issue mandates, survey requirements, and industry assessments the bill would have imposed. Seniors and disabled beneficiaries who lose coverage continue to face whatever protections state and federal law provided without this bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, but the six-senator sponsor group split 4 Republican and 2 Democratic, so the bill's visible support was bipartisan rather than partisan.

industries.note: The bill would force them to sell policies to protected applicants regardless of health, ban preexisting-condition exclusions during initial enrollment, run satisfaction surveys, and pay assessments for consumer counseling. Their interest in defeating it ran against beneficiaries' right to keep affordable coverage after losing it.

They would have to notify enrollees of their new rights when contracts end or enrollees leave, conduct consumer satisfaction surveys, disclose results, and pay their share of the counseling assessments. In exchange, beneficiaries who leave their plans would gain an easier path back to Medigap coverage, reducing a barrier to enrolling in the plans in the first place.

industries.industry: Nonprofit consumer organizations and state counseling agencies
industries.note: The bill authorizes grants to these groups to produce plain-language plan comparisons for beneficiaries, funded by industry assessments up to $35 million a year.
